plan: Complete enhanced-ACT passage set: one original humanities passage of about 700 words (CLD-P-ACT-R-000029) on how acoustic and electrical recording equipment shaped early recorded music, with 9 questions (Key Ideas and Details 4, Craft and Structure 3, Integration 2). Factual claims kept to well-documented history (acoustic horn recording before about 1925, about three minutes per side on a ten-inch 78, tuba and horn-violin substitutions, microphone-era intimate singing) and hedged where practice varied.

passages.title: What the Horn Heard
passages.text:
When people listen to the earliest recordings of music, made in the decades around 1900, they often assume they are hearing how the musicians of that era sounded. The assumption is understandable. A recording seems to be a kind of window: the performer played, the machine listened, and the result was preserved. But the machines of that period did not listen the way a person in a concert hall did, and the musicians who made records knew it. What survives is less a window than a negotiation between players and a device with strong preferences of its own.

Before about 1925, records were made acoustically. There was no microphone and no electrical amplifier. Musicians played or sang into the wide mouth of a large horn, which funneled the sound onto a thin diaphragm. The diaphragm vibrated, and a stylus attached to it cut a wavering groove into a slowly turning disc of soft wax. Everything depended on the energy of the sound itself. A loud, focused tone pushed the diaphragm hard and cut a clear groove; a soft or scattered one barely moved it.

The horn's preferences shaped the music in ways that a listener today can easily miss. Very low notes registered poorly, so the deep pulse of a string bass often vanished from the groove. Recording directors commonly replaced it with a tuba, whose blunter tone carried better. Violins, whose sound spreads in many directions, were sometimes swapped for an odd hybrid instrument that sent the strings' vibration through a metal horn of its own, aimed straight at the recording horn. Pianos were pushed close and raised on blocks. Singers with gentle voices were told to project as though addressing the back row of a theater, and to step back from the horn on their loudest notes so that they would not overload the groove.

Time was limited as well. A ten-inch disc turning at roughly seventy-eight revolutions per minute held about three minutes of music on a side. A popular song could be trimmed to fit, but a longer work could not simply be played as written. Symphonies were divided into segments, and the performers had to stop, wait for a fresh wax blank, and begin again, sometimes at a tempo a little quicker than they would have chosen in a concert, so that a movement would fit on as few sides as possible.

None of this means that early records are worthless as evidence. They preserve real details of phrasing, ornament, and pronunciation that no written score could capture, and historians of performance study them closely. But they must be read the way one reads any document produced under unusual conditions: with attention to what the conditions encouraged and what they made impossible. A forceful delivery on a disc from 1910 may tell us less about the singer's taste than about the horn the singer was standing in front of.

When electrical recording arrived, with microphones and amplifiers, the negotiation changed its terms. A microphone could catch a quiet voice from a short distance, and a new, intimate style of popular singing, soft and conversational, became possible almost at once. It is tempting to say that the technology simply freed performers to sound like themselves. Yet microphones had preferences too. They rewarded a different kind of singer, and some voices that had thrived in front of the horn sounded harsh or thin up close. Each new device, it seems, did not remove the go-between standing between performer and listener. It replaced one go-between with another, and musicians, as they always had, learned to play to it.

candidates.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.A: argue that historians should study written scores rather than early recordings of performances.
choices.B: show that early recordings reflect the demands of the recording equipment as well as the musicians' own styles.
choices.C: trace how the arrival of the microphone changed the style of popular singing after 1925.
choices.D: describe the steps by which sound was cut into a wax disc before the invention of the microphone.

candidates.evidence: What survives is less a window than a negotiation between players and a device with strong preferences of its own.
candidates.explanation: The passage argues that early records show a negotiation between musicians and the equipment: paragraphs 2-4 give the equipment's limits, paragraph 5 says how to use the records as evidence, and paragraph 6 extends the point to microphones.

A.rationale: Paragraph 5 says historians study the records closely because they preserve what scores cannot.

hints: Which choice fits every paragraph, not just one?
candidates.remember: A main-purpose answer must fit the whole passage.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, recording directors often replaced the string bass with a tuba because the tuba's sound:

choices.A: reached lower notes than a string bass could play.
choices.B: spread in many directions and so reached the horn from anywhere in the room.
choices.C: let the player stand farther from the horn without the groove overloading.
choices.D: came through to the diaphragm more strongly than the bass's deep notes did.

candidates.evidence: Recording directors commonly replaced it with a tuba, whose blunter tone carried better.
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 says low notes registered poorly and that the tuba's blunter tone carried better, so it showed up in the groove where the string bass vanished.

A.rationale: The passage says very low notes registered poorly, so lower notes would not help.

B.rationale: Spreading in many directions is what the passage says made violins hard to record.

C.rationale: The passage connects stepping back to loud singers, not to the tuba.

hints: Find the sentence that mentions the tuba.

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence before it as well.

candidates.remember: Check the sentence before a detail to see what problem it solves.

candidates.stem: The author mentions the hybrid violin in paragraph 3 mainly to:

choices.A: show how far recording sessions went to suit the horn rather than a listener.
choices.B: suggest that violinists of that period were less skilled than violinists are today.
choices.C: show that the horn favored instruments whose sound spread in many directions.
choices.D: explain why longer works such as symphonies had to be recorded in segments.

candidates.evidence: were sometimes swapped for an odd hybrid instrument
candidates.explanation: The hybrid violin is one of several changes in paragraph 3 made for the horn's sake; it shows instruments being altered to suit the machine, not the audience.

B.rationale: The passage never judges the violinists' skill.

C.rationale: The horn favored focused sound; spreading sound is why the violin was replaced.

D.rationale: Segments are explained by the time limit in paragraph 4.

hints: What do all the examples in paragraph 3 have in common?

strategy.explanation: Ask why this example is in this paragraph.

candidates.remember: A detail usually supports the claim at the start of its paragraph.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 1, the word negotiation most nearly means:

choices.A: a formal agreement reached through bargaining.
choices.B: a dispute that one side wins.
choices.D: a reluctant compromise forced on one side.

candidates.evidence: What survives is less a window than a negotiation between players and a device with strong preferences of its own.
candidates.explanation: The musicians adjusted to the device's "strong preferences", and paragraph 6 says musicians "learned to play to" each device, so negotiation means a process of mutual adjustment.

A.rationale: This is the common meaning, but no bargain or agreement is described.

B.rationale: The passage describes adjustment, not a contest with a winner.

D.rationale: The passage describes both sides shaping the result, not one side giving in.

hints: How do the musicians and the device affect each other?

strategy.explanation: Put your own word in place of negotiation, then match.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning that fits the passage, not the most common one.

candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 3, a singer with a naturally gentle voice who recorded before 1925 would most likely have been told to:

choices.A: project as if for a large hall while easing away from the horn at peak volume.
choices.B: sing softly and very close to the horn so that the diaphragm could catch every detail.
choices.C: sing in a lower range, since low notes registered most clearly in the groove.
choices.D: sing only short songs, since the horn could not record a voice for long.

candidates.evidence: Singers with gentle voices were told to project as though addressing the back row of a theater, and to step back from the horn on their loudest notes
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 says singers with gentle voices were told to project as if to the back row and to step back on loud notes so as not to overload the groove.

B.rationale: Soft, close singing became possible only with microphones (paragraph 6).

C.rationale: Paragraph 3 says very low notes registered poorly.

D.rationale: The time limit came from the disc, not the voice, and applied to all music.

hints: What two instructions does paragraph 3 give singers?
candidates.remember: An instruction can have two parts; check both.

choices.A: introduce the new technology that solved the problems described in the earlier paragraphs.
choices.B: qualify the account of distortion by explaining how early records remain useful evidence.
choices.C: add further examples of the instruments and voices that the acoustic horn recorded poorly.
choices.D: explain why historians prefer acoustic recordings to the electrical recordings that followed.

candidates.evidence: None of this means that early records are worthless as evidence.
candidates.explanation: After three paragraphs on how the horn distorted music, paragraph 5 qualifies that account: the records still hold real evidence if read with attention to the conditions that produced them.

A.rationale: That is paragraph 6, and the author says microphones did not simply solve the problems.

C.rationale: Paragraph 5 gives no new examples of instruments.

D.rationale: The paragraph does not compare acoustic and electrical recordings.

hints: How does paragraph 5 begin, and what does it push back against?

strategy.explanation: Read the first sentence of the paragraph closely.

candidates.remember: A paragraph beginning 'None of this means...' usually limits the previous claim.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must see the paragraph's role in the argument rather than its topic; the microphone choice and the 'more examples' choice catch quick readers.

candidates.stem: Based on the passage, which statement about the tempos heard in early recordings of symphonies would the author most likely accept?

choices.A: They show that orchestras of that era generally preferred quicker tempos than orchestras do today.
choices.B: They are unreliable mainly because the wax discs often warped and changed speed as they aged.
choices.C: Some may be quicker than the players' concert tempos, so they need not show the players' preferences.
choices.D: They were made slower than usual so that each segment would completely fill one side of a disc.

candidates.evidence: sometimes at a tempo a little quicker than they would have chosen in a concert
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 says some movements were played quicker to fit on fewer sides, and paragraph 5 says records must be read with attention to what the conditions encouraged. So quick tempos may reflect the disc, not the players' taste.

A.rationale: This takes the tempos at face value, which paragraph 5 warns against.

B.rationale: The passage never mentions warping or changes in speed.

D.rationale: Paragraph 4 says players sometimes went quicker, not slower, to save sides.

hints: What does paragraph 4 say about tempo, and what does paragraph 5 say about reading records?

strategy.explanation: Combine a detail from one paragraph with the principle in another.

candidates.remember: Apply the author's principle to the author's own example.

author_checklist.hardness: The answer requires combining a detail from paragraph 4 with the principle in paragraph 5; the face-value reading is a strong trap.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 6, the author's attitude toward the claim that electrical recording "simply freed performers to sound like themselves" is best described as:

choices.A: skeptical, because the new equipment rewarded some singers and not others.
choices.B: approving, because microphones could capture quiet voices from a short distance.
choices.C: dismissive, because electrical recordings were no more accurate than acoustic ones.
choices.D: uncertain, because the passage gives no information about singing after 1925.

candidates.explanation: The author calls the claim 'tempting' and then answers it with 'Yet microphones had preferences too': microphones rewarded different singers, so the claim oversimplifies.

B.rationale: The author grants this point but goes on to reject the claim.

C.rationale: The author never says electrical recordings were no more accurate.

D.rationale: Paragraph 6 describes singing after electrical recording arrived.

hints: What word introduces the author's response to the claim?

strategy.explanation: Find the sentence that begins with 'Yet'.

candidates.remember: 'It is tempting to say...' usually introduces a view the author will qualify.

author_checklist.hardness: The author first grants part of the claim; choosing between partial approval and skepticism requires reading the whole paragraph.

candidates.subskill: Applying the passage to a new situation
candidates.stem: Which of the following situations is most similar to the relationship between early performers and the recording horn, as the passage describes it?

choices.A: A painter who copies an older painting for a museum as exactly as possible, stroke by stroke
choices.B: A musician who refuses to perform anywhere except in a concert hall built for live audiences
choices.C: A sculptor who chooses marble for a statue because marble will last much longer than clay
choices.D: A speaker who adjusts gestures and pacing to suit a television camera rather than the people in the room

candidates.evidence: and musicians, as they always had, learned to play to it.
candidates.explanation: The passage's core idea is that performers shaped their playing to suit the recording device rather than the live listener. A speaker adjusting to a camera instead of the room matches that relationship.

A.rationale: Copying exactly is not adapting a performance to a device.

B.rationale: Refusing to adapt is the opposite of what the performers did.

C.rationale: Choosing a durable material is not adjusting a performance to suit a device.

hints: What did performers change, and for whose sake?

strategy.explanation: State the relationship in general terms, then match.

candidates.remember: Match the relationship, not the topic.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must abstract the passage's relationship and apply it to an unrelated field.

revision_log.reason: Round-1 blind solves (both matched every key) flagged an overreaching key in R029-07, throwaway distractors in R029-01, -04, -06 and -09, and keys echoing passage wording in R029-02, -05 and -08. Those choices were revised; the passage is unchanged. Whole batch re-solved blind.
